clue.text: What on earth? Cricket with such a bumpkin?

parts.note: a clod is a lump of earth
a cricket is a hopper, an insect that leaps

explanation.surface: A bemused onlooker wonders what a country yokel is doing on a cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cricket' looks like the English bat-and-ball game, but it is the leaping insect. 'What on' and 'with' only link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A clodhopper is a clumsy rustic, a country yokel in heavy boots.

explanation.surface: Some actors are bashful.
explanation.definitionFit: To shy is to throw or fling; the actors in a play are collectively its cast.

clue.text: Spoken of rather a lot initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the opening letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Someone is said to talk quite a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral means uttered by mouth rather than written.

clue.text: Candid play this, to follow suit

explanation.surface: A card player is urged to follow suit with a frank lead.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games, laying a heart on a heart lead is following suit, which gives the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart-to-heart talk is frank and intimate; playing one heart on another keeps to the led suit.

parts.note: a pro is someone in favour, as in pros and cons

explanation.surface: Someone supports testing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'testing' is a noun here: a proof is a trial or test, as in putting something to the proof.
explanation.definitionFit: A proof is a trial that establishes whether something holds, a test.

clue.text: Former inspector said to be in funds

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: said means spoken out, so the word for an inspector is taken by its pronunciation

parts.note: a checker is someone who inspects or checks

explanation.surface: A retired inspector is reported to be in the money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The Exchequer is the British Treasury, the government's store of public money.

explanation.surface: A plucked pheasant is offered as an example of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucked' looks like feathers removed, but it means brave.
explanation.definitionFit: Game as an adjective means brave and willing; game birds such as pheasant are hunted for sport and the table.

clue.text: A hundred and one divers outside wanting more

indicators.note: outside means the word for divers goes around the other letters

parts.note: divers is an old word for various, sundry
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Many divers gather around, greedy for more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divers' looks like swimmers but is the archaic adjective meaning several; 'outside' wraps VARIOUS round CI.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is greed, an insatiable desire for more wealth.

clue.text: Soured ale upset me first, and Edward later

indicators.note: upset means turned over, which in a down entry reads the word me from bottom to top

parts.note: bitter is a type of English ale
Ed is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: A grumpy drinker's ale upsets him, and Edward joins later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns ME into EM; BITTER is a hoppy British draught beer. 'first' and 'later' place the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Embittered means made resentful or sour in temper.

indicators.note: abused means mistreated or knocked about, so the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone named Oscar is mocked as a clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abused' rearranges the ten letters of OSCAR A MUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Scaramouch is the boastful cowardly buffoon of Italian commedia dell'arte, a stock clown figure.

explanation.surface: A two-word clue that pairs a piece of meat with a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg or shoulder of young sheep is a roasting joint; Charles Lamb was the English essayist who wrote the Essays of Elia.

clue.text: Wonder if men of fashion are seen in a street

indicators.note: are seen in means the fashionable men appear inside the other letters

parts.note: tonish is an old word for fashionable, from le bon ton, so men of fashion are tonish men

explanation.surface: People marvel at whether fashionable men appear on a certain street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if' only links; TONISH (from ton, high fashion) is rare.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonishment is a feeling of great surprise or amazement.

explanation.surface: A stuck-up person is suspected of padding out a figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: falsies are padding worn inside clothing, so the garment on top is filled out.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-important, starchy person is called this idiom; and a blouse padded with falsies is literally filled out.

indicators.note: misusing means handling wrongly, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Abusing drugs drives a person mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' belongs to the fodder: THAT DRUG IS has the ten letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Distraught means frantic or deranged with worry.

explanation.surface: A house free of ghosts is a sad place.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: a house with no ghost is without a spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dwelling free of ghosts lacks any spook; a melancholy person lacks liveliness or vigour.

clue.text: Two kids misbehaving in Latin-you are not prepared

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
a romp, in old usage, is a boisterous frolicking child, a tomboy
tu is the Latin for you

explanation.surface: Two naughty children in a Latin lesson are told they have not done their homework.
explanation.walkthrough: The one phrase supplies both children, IMP and ROMP; 'in' and 'are' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done off the cuff, without rehearsal, is impromptu.

clue.text: Puzzle contains anagram that's solved very quickly

indicators.note: contains means the word for puzzle holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: to pose is to puzzle or baffle

indicators.note: the word anagram signals that the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A crossword includes an anagram that is solved in a flash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anagram' rearranges THAT'S into THAST, which goes inside POSE; 'solved' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Posthaste means with great speed, at once.

indicators.note: the word one is split apart by the other piece, which sits between its letters

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An arithmetic statement that ten equals one over six, which is nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' points to the answer of 10 across, LAMB, read here as sheep-like; 'divided by' looks like arithmetic but puts VI inside ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovine is the adjective for sheep, so anything relating to a young sheep is ovine.

indicators.note: wrong means mistaken or out of order, so the letters of the word beside it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Continuing the sums, someone is told their division is mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue number is part of the definition: 18 divided by six gives the answer. 'you're' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighteen split into six equal parts leaves parts of the number after two.

clue.text: The peculiar virtues of French subjection

indicators.note: peculiar means odd or strange, so the letters of virtues are rearranged

parts.note: de is the French for of

explanation.surface: Strange French virtues are linked with being kept in subjection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiar' rearranges VIRTUES into SERVITU; 'The' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Servitude is the state of being subjugated, enslaved or under another's control.

parts.note: after means following or later than
thought means consideration or reflection

explanation.surface: After thinking it over, a letter writer adds a postscript.
explanation.definitionFit: A postscript is something added later, an idea that occurred once the letter was done.

clue.text: Practice takes you and me a long time

parts.note: us means you and me together
an age is a very long time

explanation.surface: A habit takes us a long while to form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means customary practice or habitual use.

parts.note: yet means nevertheless, all the same

explanation.surface: Someone admits that they can still be awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' only links; the Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas is the definition's source.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Himalayan ape-man is called the Abominable Snowman.

clue.text: The reverse of Ok, things that are cracked up

indicators.note: up in a down entry means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: nuts are cracked open to be eaten

explanation.surface: Things that have broken down are the opposite of all right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'OK' reversed is KO, a knockout, which is what the answer means; 'cracked up' suggests madness but 'up' reverses NUTS.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock someone senseless is a KO, the letters of okay turned around.

explanation.surface: A plain phrase describing a happy song.
explanation.definitionFit: A glee is an unaccompanied part-song for three or more voices; glee also means delight or merriment.

explanation.surface: Part of a flight is being watched.
explanation.definitionFit: The escapement is the mechanism in a clock or watch that regulates release of the spring's power; in old usage the word also meant an escape or flight.

clue.text: Work to take to this lecture

explanation.surface: Someone is told to take their work to a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a fill-in-the-blank: to take someone to ___ is the idiom for lecturing or rebuking them.
explanation.definitionFit: A task is a piece of work to be done; to take to task means to reprimand.

indicators.note: in disorder means jumbled up, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Parties held in a flat break up in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment, but it means dull; 'in disorder' rearranges PARTIES END.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian prose is dull and uninspired, lacking liveliness.
